content:
Lean has a mechanism called functional but in-place (FBIP).
When updating a value whose reference count is at most one, Lean can update that value destructively in place.
This is an important mechanism for optimizing program performance.
However, programmers have few ways to determine when this optimization occurs and when it does not.
They generally need to inspect the code themselves or examine the generated IR.
I therefore thought it might be useful to have a linter that identifies places where an in-place update cannot be performed because the reference count is greater than one.
What do you think?

Would implementing such a linter be difficult?

It seems that something called a stateful linter was added recently. Would stateful linters be useful for implementing this kind of linter?

Asei Inoue said:

Would implementing such a linter be difficult?

It seems that something called a stateful linter was added recently. Would stateful linters be useful for implementing this kind of linter?

Implementing a linter that always catches this is undecidable. Implementing a linter that is useful in practice has been considered several times but it's quite hard to catch all of the common mistakes that people make without false positives. It's also not really a property you can extract from the surface language but instead you have to look at the final (or almost final) IR to do it.

@Henrik Böving

Thank you for your reply.

Implementing a linter that always catches this is undecidable.

I did not realize that the problem was undecidable. I thought it might still be useful without solving the problem completely, but if even detecting common mistakes is difficult, perhaps this should not be implemented as a linter.

It's also not really a property you can extract from the surface language but instead you have to look at the final (or almost final) IR to do it.

So this is not really an issue that should be detected by a linter. However, it should be observable at runtime.

What about providing an option that, when enabled during execution, emits a warning whenever an unintended copy occurs?

In other words, I am suggesting adding a flag such as --warn-copy as an execution option for lake exe, which would emit warnings for unintended copies.

This would require some way to indicate that a particular copy is intentional, although I have not yet thought of a good mechanism for doing so.

What about providing an option that, when enabled during execution, emits a warning whenever an unintended copy occurs?

I've also considered (and implemented) this before. It does help to catch a few issues but there are also many false positives here when you just naively instrument the copying mechanism because there are copies that are sensible. For example, the compiler does common subexpression elimination where if it detects that a value is being built multiple times it will instead only built it once and then reuse it across all the previous use sites to reduce code size etc. Of course this value now might need to be copied but this is not really a bug per se. After all without the optimization you would already have allocated a copy eagerly to begin with.

@Henrik Böving

I've also considered (and implemented) this before.

Thank you. I’m glad to know that someone has been thinking about how to make FBIP easier to use.

What about using different syntax when the programmer specifically wants an update to be performed in place?

For example, instead of writing

x := x + 1

one could write something like

x ←= x + 1

Then the compiler could emit a warning if a copy occurs despite the use of this syntax.

This is something you can do yes. One issue with this is that it requires duplicating a lot of API because the copy does not happen in the := part of that but in the + part so you need to implement a copy and a non copy plus

@Henrik Böving

I see. I had not realized that the issue went that far. Duplicating the API would be a serious problem, so it seems unlikely that this approach would provide a viable solution. Thank you.

@Henrik Böving

If implementing such a linter is not feasible, another approach might be to make debugging easier by inserting dbgTraceIfShared instead.

Would it be possible to automatically insert dbgTraceIfShared at every update site of the form x := x ...?
Sure that's possible, it's also going to yield some false positives because of things like the common subexpression elimination I mentioned above but maybe people are interested in it regardless
https://github.com/hlee131/lean-hackathon-2026 has something along those lines

Also, afaik dbgTraceIfShared can produce a false positive because there’s a chance the reference count might decrease before the actual update is performed (i.e. being shared at some point does not necessarily imply being copied).

I’ve also wanted something along these lines many times :) The real thing i care about is “did I write nonperformant code by accident” (and I think that’s generally the use case people care about). So, some method of only warning (at runtime) when the copies are sufficiently big or happen too many times (maybe of anything as opposed to something I hand-annotate) would be enough, but I’m not sure if looking at it from this angle makes it easier or harder to make it reliable :upside_down:

So, some method of only warning (at runtime) when the copies are sufficiently big or happen too many times

I've done both of these and unfortunately are either too over or underapproximative for many issues in my experience.
But maybe it could be useful for easy mistakes that people commonly make? idk
i did manage to find these ones lean4#3887 lean4#3881 at the first FRO retreat with this approach

I’m guessing it’s probably not so useful when hunting for code but might be useful in the context of “I could do this a couple different ways and want to make sure my hand-written change didn’t introduce a bad sharing bug.”

Actually, I can imagine false positives there too! From the example here (common subexpression elimination), seems like the issue is “the compiler made some global optimization that messes with our local ‘probe’ while preserving global performance”. So maybe if we could somehow see that the global stats are the same or equivalent between the two versions? Show me all my allocation sizes, my copies and copy sizes, etc.? Idk.

Actually, I can imagine false positives there too!

yes you get hundreds of them

Aside from trying to be very clever about what came from the compiler and what came from the human, maybe we can just record tons of statistics and shift the problem to “tools for visualizing/inspecting/navigating dense statistics about code performance” instead of trying to make it the computer’s job to know what we want to see…a good visualization/means of inspection should be insensitive in some ways to global rearrangements due to optimizations. If such a visualization exists. :grinning_face_with_smiling_eyes:
I would say the visualization is a flamegraph and you can see pretty easily in one when a non linearity happens by looking for excessive lean_copy_expand_array most of the time.
Oh neat, does that take into account the size/cost of the copy?
Well it's going to tell you how long the copy took so sure.
There are still non linearities you wont find (namely ones not based on arrays) but most of the costly ones are based on arrays
I wonder if you could somehow make #flame cmd show a flamegraph for fully elaborating cmd in the infoview, or if you need to be outside the process :thinking:
Or if that would just be too noisy for a single command anyway

Either way I guess there are two different problems here:

  1. I’m developing some specific code and want a granular view sensitive to unexpected copying
  2. I want to hunt for unexpected copying at scale

@Henrik Böving

I would say the visualization is a flamegraph and you can see pretty easily in one when a non linearity happens by looking for excessive lean_copy_expand_array most of the time.

How can I view the flamegraph?
You need to use a C profiler of your choice, the most common one would be perf and then use e.g. hotspot or flamegraph.pl. At the FRO we mostly use samply.

Hello! I'm one of the developers of the UW hackathon project related to this issue, shared by Eric above.

From my understanding, in order to do this with a linter you would need to do something like implement a linear type system, which is not a viable approach.

What we decided to do (Jonathan Protzenko suggested the approach) was to add new syntax which, when elaborated, automatically wraps uses of a variable with dbgTraceIfShared. For the hackathon the syntax we used was let +unshared x := …, and then instrumented later let x := … x … uses as let x := … (dbgTraceIfShared … x) …. We further added a compiler option that controlled whether let +unshared gets elaborated this way or not (so you can selectively enable the instrumentation only in test environments, and keep it off in production).

We didn't quite finish some of the details of the elaboration by the end of the hackathon, but if there's interest in this feature I'd be happy to submit a PR to get feedback and finish it.

This approach is susceptible to false positives, but I think that those can be reduced somewhat (if not completely). I believe this approach would work best in a test suite to ensure that intentionally optimized algorithms retain the intended optimizations.

Profiling seems like the best approach for finding algorithms that are worth optimizing in the first place.

@Derrik Petrin

Hi! Thanks for your message.

I’m very interested in that feature.

Isn’t the false positive issue a serious problem?
Is implementing linear types and building a linter theoretically impossible, or is it simply difficult or tedious?

I don’t know about the general computational complexity. Henrik said above that it’s undecidable in general here which I would not be surprised by. It is at the very least a masters thesis level of work to implement a linear type system. Leveraging the existing runtime checks is certainly the lowest effort path.
I’ll take a look at the two performance optimizations Henrik linked above and apply my check against the before and after versions to see what the false positives look like and report back.

The undecidability quite simply follows from the fact that you are asking arbitrary aliasing question in a turing complete language. If you use things like linear type systems you can of course lock yourself into a fragment that ends up working. There is prior work on this here https://pp.ipd.kit.edu/uploads/publikationen/huisinga23masterarbeit.pdf and while this does end up with a system that works at the IR level its quite unclear at the moment how one would implement a nice type theory affinity and borrowing that works at the surface level language (I.e. with dependent types etc)

@Henrik Böving @Marc Huisinga

Thank you for pointing me to this excellent paper.

It seems that the paper was published in 2023, but the ideas presented in it have not been implemented in Lean as it exists today, correct?

The paper goes as far as describing an implementation of uniqueness types, so I assume their feasibility has already been demonstrated. Are there any obstacles to integrating them into the Lean compiler?
I'll let marc comment on the details but the short summary is that what Marc ended up with is nowhere close where we'd want this to be for proper support in Lean.
